1128.note: The editor's description, re-read in the archive.org full text on 16 Nov 2026, Klinckowström, Le comte de Fersen et la cour de France I (1877), p. 155 note to no. CXXXVII: the Empress's extract 'est ajouté comme apostille à la lettre en chiffre (non déchiffrée) du roi de Suède Gustave III au comte de Fersen, datée de Stockholm, le 28 février 1792'. The edition marks other Gustav III letters 'd'après la lettre originale, déchiffrée dans les papiers du comte de Fersen', so 'non déchiffrée' means no decipherment was found with this one. Fersen surely read it in 1792, and his diary or Proschwitz's 1986 edition of Gustav III's letters may give its sense. Neither could be checked, hence medium confidence. Note: the editor's note sits on p. 155, not p. 156.

II/8 (1982), p. 405, says Menzel's letter of 23/13 Sept 1633 (fol. 83-84) is 'größtenteils in Chiffre, deren Auflösung jedoch fehlt'. 2217.note: The edition question is closed: no edition prints c. 13r. This pass searched Lorenzo de' Medici, Lettere V (1480-81), VI (1481-82) and VII (1482-84) inside the archive.org copies through the full-text search service (bwb_KU-999-230_5, bwb_KU-999-229_6, bwb_KU-999-231; query 'GC, 137'). These volumes cite eight GC 137 pieces, all letters to Niccolò Michelozzi: V cc. 32-33 and 47 (31 Jan 1481) and cc. 20-21 (3 Jul 1481); VI cc. 6-9 (5 Aug 1481), cc. 45-46 (5 Nov 1481) and c. 4 (28 Jan 1482); VII cc. 22-23, 26 and 35 (28 Aug 1482), cc. 48-51 (29 Oct 1483) and cc. 38-39 (7 Apr 1484). No 'c. 13' and no 'biglietto' appears in any of them. This confirms the 9 Nov Censimento check (research/vetting_2026-11/out_c32.json). What stops a verdict is the question left open on 9 Nov. The clear strip c. 12r (BNCF0003827893, re-fetched and read this pass) is the same size and layout as the cipher strip c. 13r (BNCF0003827895): four lines, about 261 letters against about 263 signs. Its text runs 'El conte Girolamo ha sollecitato l'andata di m. Ascanio a Roma ... el S. L[odovi]co et m. palavisino et strasoldano è sospecto assai parendo loro che lui sia di ghibellini'. It may be the decipherment or the draft of c. 13r. One observation this pass points that way. The cipher's near-repeat '5 g 5 3 n (m) π b t' comes once at the end of line 1 and once mid line 3. The clear has 'S. Lco et' twice ('opera del S. Lco et', 'tra S. Lco et'). In the second cipher occurrence the repeat is followed by 'm', and the clear has 'm. palavisino' at that point. With code signs for names compressing the early text, the positions fit. No sign table was rebuilt, so this is suggestive, not proof. If c. 12r is the plaintext, the verdict is read (contemporary clear). If a homophonic attack with c. 12r as crib fails, it is open.

2449.note: The archive's own title, re-read on AIS 16 Nov 2026, is 'Ajalugu. Ülestähend. M. Sild. 1905-1906 Avinurmes (salakirjas)', 19 leaves, dated 1907, with no digital object and no decipherment or transcription in the unit or the series. In Estonian 'salakiri' means secret writing or cipher. Shorthand would be 'kiirkiri' and a Gothic hand 'gooti kiri', so the earlier doubt (shorthand or Gothic) is weaker than recorded. The title still does not prove a cipher, and the item is a private 1907 account outside diplomatic scope, hence low confidence. The same series holds Sild's clear 'Seletus' on the breaking of the Tsar's portraits (AM.272.1.96) and the indictment (AM.272.1.95). These are not the same text (the cipher account covers 1905-1906), but they would give names and events as cribs.

2901.recommendation: keep as a low-priority lead (code-book search); do not promote
2901.note: My judgement is to keep this as a lead and not promote it. Waves 15-16 screened HIL/64 and HIL/65 completely and tallied about 133 Sudan Government telegrams carrying dictionary code words inside clear English (wave16_durham README, code-word tally). The words are bare, with no decode on any form. They belong to a code book, not a cipher: they come from several languages (Latin Aglossa, German Alantapfel, Spanish Agazapada, Italian Acquitrino), in the manner of the Berne Official Vocabulary (1894) on which private codes were built. They stand for stock items: months (64/136 'Fissurum (January) to Flaccidus (March)'), persons ('Adulterino (Khedive)', 64/296 and 65/961), offices, ranks, decoration classes and set phrases. The two meanings that the forms themselves give confirm this. There is nothing to cryptanalyse. With the Sudan Government's telegraph code every word reads at once; without it only a partial reconstruction from context is possible, and the payoff is stock phrases inside telegrams whose sense is already clear. No code book has been found: HIL/149-155 are Ottoman, Arabic and French codes of the Khedive's own circle (wave 18), HIL/149 is not digitised, and the Sudan Railway code SAD.969/15 dates from 1937. A web search for Agyllinos, Aginaverid and Alantapfel found no printed code listing them. The real cipher in these files is already handled: HIL/64/890-891 and HIL/65/148, 157-158 are leads 2899 and 2900 (key_lookup, clear copies on file), and HIL/64/400, HIL/65/273 and HIL/65/1122 are catalogue 2907-2909. Catalogue 2909 sits beside the code words 'Aglossa' and 'fistularia', so a found code book would also help there. Without a verdict I give no vetting block: the gate's 'open' is meant for an unread cipher, and this lead's reading depends on finding a book, not on solving.

Next step: look for the Sudan Government telegraph code of c. 1907-1914 in the Durham Sudan Archive (Wingate, Slatin papers; SAD.451/124/73 'cipher amendments' 1909), TNA FO 141 / WO 33 / FO 371 Egypt, and the printed private codes based on the Berne Vocabulary.
